findings.passage: Read in order, his own essays show a man who gives up titles with unusual ease. The one stretch where he describes himself stuck for years is the one where he had nothing to point to.
findings.problem: The framing sentence misdescribes the 2019 essay (reopened via an archived copy; the live blog returned HTTP 522). The three stalled years (2015 to 2018) were the years he built Gym, Universe and the Dota environment, which he says drew "the team's excitement every time I overcame a new obstacle" and felt "deeply validating" (the draft quotes this itself). "Nothing to show" covers only the July 2017 behavioral-cloning side project. The essay's own explanation for the stall runs the other way: "my software skills were always in demand, and I kept procrastinating on picking up the machine learning skills I wanted." By his account he stayed stuck while he had plenty to point to. This sentence sets up the title, description and type argument, so a reader who opens the essay will find the premise false.
findings.acceptance_test: The sentence, and any echo in the title, description or FAQ, matches the essay. The multi-year stall coexisted with visible, praised infrastructure work, and "nothing to show" is tied to the single 2017 project. The article quotes or paraphrases the essay's "always in demand ... procrastinating" explanation and says whether it helps or hurts the Three reading. Staying where you are already valued could be a Three move, but it is not having "nothing to point to."

findings.passage: He came back in private, over a holiday, beside someone who made failure feel "ok," and he scored the comeback in commits and hours. That is the Type 3 fear in plain form: failing where people can see it.
findings.problem: The draft says this essay carries most of the type argument, yet this paragraph's causal story leaves out the essay's counterevidence. (1) The hook cuts the "correct them" sentence mid-thought. In full: "People would mention how how hard behavioral cloning from human data is. I always made sure to correct them by pointing out that I was a newbie, and this probably said more about my abilities than the problem." Colleagues offered him a face-saving explanation, and he publicly turned it down and blamed his own ability. That is close to the opposite of protecting how failure looks, and the draft never weighs it. (2) The essay gives non-image reasons for the timing. He started again in November 2018 because "the demands on my time had relented" after The International, and he persisted "because I didn't want to be constrained to only understanding one part of my projects. I wanted to see the whole picture clearly." "In private" is the author's word, not his. (3) The hours figure measures his motivation ("the number of hours I can motivate myself to spend"), not a visible result. The commits that made him proud were Pachocki's and Sidor's. (4) The next paragraph's discriminator, "A One's block tends to center on doing it wrong; his centered on others' estimate of him," conflicts with the essay. His listed frustrations are about doing it wrong: "small bugs that had been corrupting my results the whole time," not knowing "which code a given experiment had used," and being "too timid" to "make substantive changes to someone else's machine learning code."
findings.acceptance_test: The hook or this section quotes the full "...said more about my abilities than the problem" sentence and deals with it. The paragraph gives the essay's own reasons (time freed after The International in 2018; wanting to "see the whole picture clearly") and engages them. The One-versus-Three sentence acknowledges the error-centered frustrations. "That is the Type 3 fear in plain form" is either defended against these four points with a specific, sourced reason or recast as one labeled reading. If the essay can no longer separate Three from One, the evidence record's discriminator and confidence (C85, C86, C109) are updated to say so.

findings.passage: On the stand, he described the line he would not cross in 2017 as one that would "serve the mission" but be hard to face in the mirror.
findings.problem: This item is counted as evidence that he picks results over rightness, but it shows the reverse. In November 2017 he called an act "pretty morally bankrupt" even though, by his May 2026 gloss (MIT Technology Review, May 8, 2026), it "would actually serve the mission." Rejecting something that serves the goal because of how it would be done is means over ends, which is the One pattern. "The diary and the mirror" already concedes that the idiom fits either type, yet the item is used here as a Three discriminator. The paragraph's other items are weaker than presented. A launch rule under which he has "never missed a hard" date is commitment-keeping, not a principle traded for speed. The March 2020 peer review accused a colleague of "abusing her power," a fairness charge the evidence record itself files under the Type 1 case (C32). The draft also omits the WSJ's next line, that Altman read it beforehand and called it "tough but fair," and that the fight was over "warring feedbacks" after Daniela Amodei rebutted him "point by point." Once those items are discounted, the claim that he "keeps turning up on the other side" from procedure rests mainly on one anonymous Fortune quote.
findings.acceptance_test: The mirror item is removed from the Three side of the discriminator, or the article argues explicitly why a means-constraint still favors Three. The peer-review item is presented with "tough but fair" and the two-sided dispute, and treated as cutting both ways. The section names at least one dated, non-anonymous instance where he gave up a stated principle or procedure for speed or results at a real cost. If no such instance exists, the section says the discriminator rests mainly on anonymous testimony, and confidence language in the body, FAQ and evidence record drops to match.

findings.passage: The rival case deserves its strongest form.
findings.problem: The section promises the One case in its strongest form, but it leaves out the most One-like evidence already in the research record. (1) The New Yorker (April 6, 2026) quotes a second 2017 diary entry stating a truthfulness rule: "cannot say that we are committed to the non-profit . . . if three months later we're doing b-corp then it was a lie." (2) The 2014 essay opens: "I had a very strong vision of the environment I wanted to be a part of, and I was willing to go out of my way to make it exist." (3) Asked in April 2026 how he operates, he said much the same thing again: "I also really care about the environment in which these things are done." He described giving up "type one fun" for work that is "painful in the moment, but it's worthwhile," adding "you really do have to be willing to take on great personal pain" (The Knowledge Project, about 27:48 to 28:22). A twelve-year self-description of building the right environment, plus a diary rule against public commitments that would become "a lie," is the One case at its strongest. Neither "If he is a One" nor "Where the One reading strains" mentions it.
findings.acceptance_test: "If he is a One" includes the "it was a lie" diary line and at least one of the 2014 or 2026 environment self-descriptions, each sourced and dated, and the evidence record gains matching claims. "Where the One reading strains" either gives a specific reason these items fit Three better or says plainly that they favor One.

findings.passage: He picked a field by where he could be best, and his favorite early story is about dedication that someone noticed and rewarded with a role built for him.
findings.problem: This misstates the source's logic, and it is thesis evidence (C64). In the Stratechery interview, "best in the world" was his bar for committing to anything. The choice between acting and the hard sciences was about impact: "I ended up picking the hard sciences one, because I felt like maybe that was an area where I could most make a difference in the world." The draft quotes that line one paragraph earlier and then summarizes it the other way. "Favorite early story" is unsupported: he offered it as one of "two stories" when asked about North Dakota. His own gloss stresses the job's single requirement ("this job has one requirement, which is you're going to be six hours at attention") and "trying to find creative ways to get" the job done. That conscientiousness reading is as available to a One as the noticed-and-rewarded reading is to a Three.
findings.acceptance_test: The summary sentence matches the source. It describes the field choice as based on impact ("most make a difference"), and it drops "favorite" or sources it. His own gloss on the gingerbread story (the one requirement, getting the job done) appears beside the noticed-and-rewarded reading. C64's inference is revised to match.

findings.passage: He rarely fights for titles, and after Altman became CEO in 2019 he took "a less public-facing role," as Fortune put it.
findings.problem: The draft presents as a trait (title humility, "light on glamour") a change the cited record describes as imposed. The WSJ piece the draft already cites says Altman and Dario Amodei agreed employees "didn't have faith in Brockman and Sutskever's leadership," and that "Dario agreed to stay so long as Altman promised that Brockman and Sutskever wouldn't be in charge. Altman agreed." The New Yorker says Altman "assured some researchers that Brockman's managerial authority would be diminished." On the language project, the WSJ says he "wanted a role," "appealed to Altman," and then "Brockman and Altman reluctantly agreed to keep Brockman off the language project." So he did fight for a role, and lost. The draft misreads the episode in both directions. Here, the 2019 step back is read as modesty. In the Nine paragraph, the same record becomes "pushing onto a project over its leaders' objections," even though the source says he accepted being kept off.
findings.acceptance_test: Wherever the 2019 "less public-facing role" appears (body and C40), the article says that colleagues' reported loss of confidence and Altman's assurances came first. It is no longer evidence of title humility unless that context is weighed. In the Nine paragraph, "pushing onto a project over its leaders' objections" is replaced with what the WSJ reports: he sought the role, appealed to Altman, then agreed to stay off. The rebuttal of Type 9 is re-checked without the overstated item.

findings.passage: What the record shows most consistently is a man who measures himself by work that lands.
findings.problem: The closing claim rests on a chain of quotes, and each is cut just before he states an intrinsic or service motive. The draft quotes 2015's "the deep satisfaction of having others actually use my creations" but drops the sentence before it: "I originally got hooked on programming because I loved the act of creating something from nothing." In 2017, "These are the times I feel most alive" continues "coding feels like magic made real, where anything I can imagine and describe becomes possible." In Stratechery, "It was the most glorious feeling" is followed in the evidence excerpt by "I want to help people, I want to benefit people and build for them." In 2014 he chose to return to coding as "energy management" and "activities that recharge you (independent of leverage)," the least visible of the four options he listed. Restore those clauses and the most consistent thread is love of building and of impact, which a builder of almost any type would share. Words like "validating" don't distinguish types. This is the Enneagram 6 anchor's failure: an argument that could describe any ambitious engineer.
findings.acceptance_test: Each trimmed quote either keeps its motive clause or sits beside the intrinsic or service motive it came with. The "most consistently" claim is then argued against the craft and impact alternatives with at least one sourced detail a craft- or impact-driven builder would not show, or it is softened to a labeled interpretation (C117).

findings.passage: The stated reason is the effect on OpenAI and its people, and the message as reported does not call the giving wrong.
findings.problem: The super PAC reversal is used as a discriminator ("His latest reversal fits") without testing the obvious rival explanation, which is audience and incentive. Gizmodo (October 1, 2026) frames the message as an internal Slack from the company's president, sent "following intense backlash." It also reports OpenAI's June statement that his involvement was "in a personal capacity, not on behalf of the company," and rank-and-file employees giving "more than $200,000" to a counterweight super PAC. Any executive would frame that message around company impact, and putting in writing that one's own political giving was wrong would be a liability. So the missing moral word doesn't discriminate between types. The quote also drops its middle sentence, "I've been thinking hard about how to turn the ship on it," with no ellipsis. The type FAQ hardens the report into a cause ("because it kept 'reflecting on the company'") and omits "distraction for people here." Gizmodo also attributes the $50 million pledge to Brockman "and his wife."
findings.acceptance_test: The section mentions the reported backlash and employee dissent and marks the omitted Slack sentence. It names audience and role incentives as an explanation before drawing any type inference. The "Why isn't Greg Brockman a Type 1?" FAQ either quotes both stated reasons or drops "because." The pledge attribution matches the source. The item stays in the discriminator only if the article explains why it discriminates despite the incentive explanation. Otherwise it is labeled non-discriminating, and stays so until WIRED (S21) or the Times original is opened.

findings.passage: Still, separate outlets describe the same tendency: speed over process.
findings.problem: The ends-over-means case leans on anonymous Fortune quotes. Meanwhile, the most-reported named and documented episode on exactly that question is left out, with no explanation in the article. The New Yorker, citing "several interviews and contemporaneous records," and the WSJ both report a 2017 idea to sell or auction AGI to governments; the WSJ says to the UN Security Council's nuclear powers. Page Hedley, on the record, recalls that "Greg kept going back to 'So how do we raise more money? How do we win?'" Brockman's response is also on record: he "never seriously entertained auctioning A.I. models to governments," and he calls any larger characterization "utterly ridiculous." Separately, under oath in May 2026 he admitted telling early donors to give $100,000 personally and never doing so himself (Courthouse News via the evidence excerpt; that site blocked automated access for this review). The draft includes rival-sourced and anonymous material but leaves out named adverse evidence. The result is a profile that looks gentler on Brockman, and a Three case that looks weaker, than the record supports. This falls under the sensitive_allegations risk.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the article presents the governments episode with named attribution (Hedley; WSJ and New Yorker), its disputed status and Brockman's denial, weighted as contested, or the evidence record documents why it is excluded and the discriminator stops relying on anonymous same-camp items that are no stronger. Either way, the sworn $100,000 admission is either weighed on the image-versus-conduct question or excluded with a stated reason.

findings.passage: His first vacation became a build.
findings.problem: This is a context-fidelity problem. The 2014 essay says he took "a vacation (my first ever) to Hawaii, and then holed myself up with a few engineers building CTF3." The two happened in sequence, and he calls both "the best thing I did" toward "making sure people would take their problems to Marc rather me" (sic). That makes it a deliberate delegation tactic, not rest turning into work. "Like a bear" then builds on that misreading ("rest that turns into more building") and leaves out his stated reason for the 2024 break. After Sutskever left, he said, "I needed some time to kind of find my way back to remembering like why I was doing this, and why it was so important, and why it was worth the pain" (The Knowledge Project, about 24:00). He describes a loss of meaning, not depletion.
findings.acceptance_test: The Stripe sentence keeps the "and then" sequence and his stated delegation purpose. The sabbatical paragraph includes his own stated reason. The "rest only after depletion" loop is re-tested against both.

findings.passage: Ten years after admiring the pronouncement, he was the one making it.
findings.problem: The closing bookend is an attractive symmetry the sources don't support. In 2016 he admired someone announcing a goal not yet reached. In 2026, as launch spokesman, he declared at a launch briefing that a goal had been met. In his own Stratechery words that claim was hedged ("maybe it was the previous model, maybe it's Astra, maybe it's the next model"), and it remains contested. Ending the portrait there implies a motive (wanting to be the bold announcer) that the article never argues, and it ties the conclusion to a time-sensitive product claim.
findings.acceptance_test: Either the bookend goes, or the closing labels the 2026 line as launch messaging, includes his hedge and says what it does and doesn't show about motive. The ending's point survives if the AGI claim is later disputed or withdrawn.

protected_passages.passage: The next line sits alone as its own paragraph: "I never tried machine learning on the Dota project again."
protected_passages.reason: Verified against the archived essay: the sentence is its own paragraph. This is a sourced, specific, memorable hook. Restoring the full "correct them" sentence (critic-02) does not require changing it.

protected_passages.passage: This was the costliest choice in his record, made in an afternoon, and it is the One reading's best day: a moral verdict, with anger set aside. A Six would read it as loyalty. Nothing in it favors a Three over a One.
protected_passages.reason: This concedes the costliest choice in his record to the rivals. It matches the Knowledge Project transcript ("It just wasn't right" / "No. I felt like I understood what had happened"). Keep it as the model for how the repaired discriminator should treat adverse evidence.

protected_passages.passage: Even the charter aside cuts both ways: the care to get the lines "exactly right" belongs to a One, and the reflex to head off the impression that he had crammed belongs to a Three.
protected_passages.reason: A precise reading of one sourced detail that credits both hypotheses, the opposite of the convenient absorption flagged elsewhere.

protected_passages.passage: Sutskever also testified that his written claim that Brockman "was essentially fired from Stripe" rested on "Mira told me," meaning [Mira Murati](/personality-analysis/mira-murati), and that he never checked it with Brockman, whose 2015 farewell post describes a voluntary exit.
protected_passages.reason: Checked against the deposition transcript ("Mira told me" / "Did you seek to verify it with Greg?" "No.") and the Leaving Stripe post. A fair, sourced rebuttal of a damaging secondhand claim.

protected_passages.passage: Nothing in the record points to a formative wound, and this profile won't supply one.
protected_passages.reason: An honest refusal to invent a childhood cause, which the standard requires and the record supports.

assessment: Critic pass. The draft does several things well. It labels anonymous and rival-sourced material, concedes November 17, 2023 to the rival types, rebuts the unverified Stripe-firing claim with the deposition, and refuses to invent a childhood wound. The weakness is the causal spine. I reopened the 2019 ML essay and the 2014, 2015, 2016 and 2017 essays (archived copies; the live blog returned 522), plus Fortune, Gizmodo, the WSJ syndication, the New Yorker, MIT Technology Review's trial report, Stratechery, the Knowledge Project auto-transcript and the Sutskever deposition. Read against those sources, the Three-over-One discriminator is much weaker than the article claims. The central essay is trimmed where it cuts against the reading (critic-01, critic-02). The mirror testimony describes a means-constraint but is counted as ends over means (critic-03). One-favoring items already in the record are missing from the rival case (critic-04). The field choice is misread (critic-05). An apparently imposed 2019 step back is read as humility (critic-06). The quotes behind 'work that lands' are cut before their motive clauses (critic-07). What remains is an anonymous Fortune quote and a corporate Slack message that audience incentives explain (critic-08), and the named adverse testimony is omitted (critic-09). If repairs cannot produce a sourced, non-anonymous discriminator, the honest outcome is lower confidence or insufficient_evidence, not medium-confidence Type 3. If the lead type or the thesis changes in editing, the run should hold for --refresh --expanded-review. Similarity advisory: the Tiger Woods match ('Type 3 is organized around...') and the Margaret Qualley 'public record' match are type-definition and disclaimer boilerplate, not reused argument, so no reuse finding. The argument itself is specific to Brockman. Limits: Courthouse News blocked automated access, Axios returned 403 (I relied on the evidence excerpts), and WIRED (S21) and the New York Times original behind Gizmodo were not opened. Risks: sensitive allegations (memo, bullying claim, political giving, governments episode) and contested typing.
